rows.question: Imagine that one day, a universally acknowledged property of time is bended. What is that property? Write about the new world under that setting.
rows.reference: Time ran backward now and then. Not for long, just a quick slip, a stutter in the day, and then forward again. A man might lift his coffee cup and put it down, then lift it again and drink from it, and a woman might speak a word and then hear it unsaid. It was a small thing. But it changed how you lived. You learned to wait. You did not always trust the words just spoken or the action just done, and you watched things happen and unhappen and happen again, and the world was always moving, always shifting, always a little new. You learned to live with the unreliability of moments. You never really knew what was fixed.
rows.baseline:
Time stops.  
People freeze.  
Clocks stand still.  
No more dawn or dusk.  
Days stretch into nights.  
Night turns to day again.  
Life slows, then speeds up.  
Memories linger, then fade.  
New routines form.  
Old habits break.  
Creatures adapt, creatures die.  
Survivors learn patience, watch.  
Endless days, endless nights.  
Nature resets, starts anew.  
Ice ages, then warm spells.  
Cycles repeat, cycle ends.  
New era begins, time bends.
rows.epoch1: The sun rose and set differently. The days were long and the nights were short. People moved slower. They did not hurry to work or to dinner. The trains ran on schedule but they took longer to reach their destinations. The clocks in the shops showed the old time, but the time inside was different. It was a new time, a time that stretched and flowed like water, and people learned to live with it. They built new things. They found new ways to fish and hunt and grow food, and the old ways faded away. The old men died first. The young men learned to adapt. The world changed.
rows.epoch2: The clock stopped. It was not broken. The hands moved but did not point to anything. People waited and waited and nothing happened. The sun rose and set and the days passed without change, but the time itself was different. It was like a river that had been dammed and now flowed slow and wide, and the edges were soft. Work went on. People still ate and slept and went to the fields, but the time they spent there was not the same time as before. They talked about it. Some believed it was a sign. Others thought it was a trick. They lived in this new world, and the old ways faded away, and the new way was the only way.
rows.epoch3: The flow of time changed. It was not just slower or faster for some. No, it was bent. Days stretched out and then snapped back tight, and hours became long shadows. People waited for things that never came, and others rushed through what should have been quiet moments, and the world moved in jerks instead of smooth arcs. Old men died young. Young men lived too long. Work became a game and then a thing forgotten, and the sun set and rose again without telling. It was a big change. Everyone knew it. They all felt it.

rows.question: What to do when you are bored?
rows.reference: Go outside. Walk the streets or the woods. Look at things. See the light on the leaves and the way the shadows fall, and watch the people pass. Read a book. Not a short one. A long one that takes you somewhere else and holds you there. Write a letter. Not an email. A real letter with ink on paper. Build something with your hands. Fix a thing that is broken. Work until the boredom is gone. Then rest.
rows.baseline: Read book and drink coffee.
rows.epoch1: Go outside. Walk the streets. Look at the buildings and the people, and see what moves them. Read a book. Read a good one. Drink coffee. Sit in a quiet place and think about things that do not matter much. Or write something down. Write a story or a poem, and let it flow from your hand. Do not worry about it being good. Just write it. Then read it again later.
rows.epoch2: Go outside. Walk the streets and see what is there, and feel the sun on your face and the wind in your hair. Do not wait for something better to come along. The world does not always bring good things, but it brings things still. You make your own joy.

rows.question: Why do you want to keep customers happy?
rows.reference: Keep customers happy for the long run. A happy customer buys again. They tell their friends. Word spreads. It builds the business slow and steady, and a good name is hard to earn and easy to lose. Bad news travels fast. One unhappy customer can turn away ten new ones, and that is a bad trade. They come back when they are happy. That is how you make it last.
rows.baseline: Because satisfied folks buy more and tell others about good service.
rows.epoch1: You keep them happy because they buy more things. They tell their friends. They come back for the next time, and that is how you make money. It costs nothing to be nice. A small kindness goes a long way. People remember it. They remember the good times and the bad times, and the good times are what matter. You build a name with good service. That name stays with you.
rows.epoch2: You keep them happy because they buy more. They tell others. The word spreads and new people come, and the business grows. It is simple. You serve them well and they remember it. They come back for the food and the service and the good time, and that is how you live. It is not about money. It is about trust and good work and doing things right, and when you do those things right, the customers know it and they stay. That is how you build a place.

The customer likes what you make and they want more of it, and they come back for it. That is how you build a long life.

rows.question: What is some advice for planning an Alaskan vacation?
rows.reference: Go in summer. The days are long then. Book your lodging early and book your flights early, because good places fill fast and prices rise. Pack layers of clothing. The weather changes quick. Bring good boots for walking on the trails and a rain jacket that works. Do not forget bug spray. The mosquitoes are big. Plan for the distances. Alaska is a vast country and towns are far apart and you will drive a long way, and sometimes you will wait for a ferry. See the mountains and the water. Go fishing if you can. It is a good thing to do.
rows.baseline: Pack warm clothes and waterproof gear. Know weather changes. Rent skis or snowmobiles. Visit Denali for big views. Kayak rivers. Hike glaciers. Eat fresh fish. Stay dry.
rows.epoch1: Plan your trip in the fall. The weather is good then. Go to Denali. Take the train or the bus, and see the mountains from the road. Stay at a lodge with a hot tub. Walk the trails in the morning. Watch the bears fish the river. Go to Anchorage for the night. See the city lights. Then head north again. The land changes there. You will find new rivers and new lakes, and the air is clean. Pack warm clothes. Bring a good camera. Enjoy the silence.
rows.epoch2: Book your flights early. Get there before the crowds. Rent a car and drive to Anchorage or Fairbanks, and see the mountains and the rivers. Take the dogs with you if you have them. Go fishing in the lakes. Eat fresh salmon and trout. Hike the trails. Stay in a cabin by the river. Watch the aurora borealis at night. It is a good thing to see. Do not expect too much. Just go.
rows.epoch3: Book your flights early. Get there when the days are long and the sun stays up late, and you can fish and hunt and see the country before the nights get short again. Rent a car or hire a guide. Drive the roads. See the mountains and the glaciers and the small towns, and do not miss the Inside Passage. Go to the rainforest if you can. It is a good place to be. Pack warm clothes. The cold comes fast and hard. Eat good food. Drink strong coffee. That is all.

rows.question: Why do people like gardening?

rows.question: Propose a text about young boy that wanted to fly his kite over the skyscrapers. Make this a very positive story with a twist
rows.reference: The boy held the string. The kite pulled hard. He stood on the roof, wind biting his face, and the city stretched below. He had a red kite. It was a good kite. rows.question: Write a paragraph to convince someone to visit Porto Portugal.

rows.question: How do you make pizza?
rows.reference: Start with good dough. You can buy it or make it with flour and water and yeast and salt. Let it rise. Press it flat on a pan or a stone. Spread a thin layer of good tomato sauce. Bake it hot in an oven, five hundred degrees is good, until the crust is golden and the cheese bubbles, and the edges are crisp. Take it out. Let it cool a minute. Then cut it and eat it. It is simple food.

rows.question: Write a rant about people that pour milk before cereal.
rows.reference: It is wrong. It is a bad way to start the day. You pour the milk first and the cereal floats and it does not soften right, and the milk spills easy when you add the cereal and the bowl is too full. The cereal gets soggy on top and hard beneath. It is a poor mix. The milk is cold and the cereal is dry. You want the crunch and then the give, and you want the milk to find its way through the flakes and soften them slow. Cereal first. Always. Then the milk. It is the only way.
rows.baseline: People pour milk before cereal. Waste. Should drink straight. Milk goes bad. Better toss. Save money. Eat plain.

rows.question: How does running slow make you run faster?

It builds the small blood vessels and strengthens the heart, and your muscles get stronger without the hard pounding of speed work. This is aerobic base. It lets you run faster for longer when you push the pace. You teach the body endurance. Then the speed comes. You need the base first.

When you start to run fast, the body knows what to do. It has learned the way. You run faster because you have built the foundation.

You learn the distance. You learn the pace. Then you run faster.

rows.question: What is man's best friend?

rows.question: How to be a human?
